question: A 70-year-old man presents with progressive painless visual loss. Slit-lamp examination shows a white lens with NO visible iris shadow on oblique illumination. Which stage of senile cataract does this represent?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Immature cataract shows a POSITIVE iris shadow (shadow falls on the pupil) because the anterior cortex is still partially transparent.

Correct. In mature cataract the entire lens is opaque — no iris shadow is cast because there is no transparent zone anterior to the opacity. The absence of iris shadow (negative iris shadow test) is the hallmark.
Hypermature/Morgagnian cataract also lacks an iris shadow, but additionally shows liquefied cortex with a sunken brown nucleus visible through the anterior capsule — not described here.
Lamellar cataract is a developmental/congenital type affecting a specific zone; it is not part of the senile maturation sequence.

overallFeedback.feedback: The iris shadow test is decisive. No shadow with a totally white lens points to mature cataract. Revisit the stages of senile cataract maturation.
Well done. A white lens with NO iris shadow = mature cataract. Remember: iris shadow PRESENT = immature; iris shadow ABSENT = mature or hypermature.
